title: How to read an ECB energy scenario with no extra policy response
summary: The most consequential qualification in the 19 March press conference came in its final answer. The ECB’s adverse energy scenarios included no extra monetary-policy response beyond the path anticipated by markets at the baseline cut-off. Investors could use those exercises to see what a more intense or persistent shock might do to inflation and growth under a common policy assumption. Translating a higher scenario inflation number directly into a forecast of where inflation would land after the ECB had responded would misread the exercise. The Council had unanimously kept rates unchanged while retaining the ability to adjust them.

The timing of the projections mattered almost as much as their design. Staff first completed a baseline as of 4 March, then produced a new one incorporating news through 11 March. The latter was the Council’s published central case. Headline inflation averaged 2.6% in 2026, 2.0% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028. Inflation excluding energy and food was 2.3%, 2.2% and 2.1%. Lagarde said the last number incorporated the assumed introduction of ETS2 in 2028 as well as residual base and second-round effects. A small overshoot at the end of the horizon therefore had several sources. Growth averaged 0.9%, 1.3% and 1.4% in the three years, reflecting damage to real incomes, confidence and spending.

In the adverse scenario, oil and gas prices rose substantially above the baseline and converged back toward the earlier 4 March path around the end of the projection horizon. In the severe scenario, prices rose somewhat more and stayed elevated long enough for convergence to occur beyond the horizon. The time spent at expensive energy, and the number of price or pay decisions made during that time, could matter as much as the initial jump. Lagarde identified the indicators she wanted to monitor. These included commodity markets, supply bottlenecks, selling-price expectations, the frequency of firms’ price revisions, purchasing managers’ surveys, consumer confidence and wage trackers. Together they could distinguish the shock itself from the build-up of more persistent inflation.

The comparison with 2022 put concrete limits on extrapolation. Lagarde recalled inflation being around 6% when the earlier shock struck, against a latest reading of 1.9% in the current episode. Labour shortages and workers’ bargaining position had also been stronger then, and pent-up spending had added a demand shock. On the other hand, recent experience of high inflation could now influence wage negotiations and corporate pricing sooner. The new baseline already contained some indirect and secondary effects, partly based on judgement. The choice therefore concerned the size and speed of additional propagation. A simple assumption of either a full repeat or a complete absence of the earlier dynamics would omit information the Council itself identified.

February prices still largely described the economy entering the shock. Inflation excluding energy and food rose from 2.2% in January to 2.4% in February. Goods inflation reached 0.7% and services 3.4%. Compensation per employee had slowed from 4.0% growth in the third quarter to 3.7% in the fourth. Wage indicators pointed to further moderation. Market-based near-term inflation expectations had increased considerably, while most longer-term measures remained around 2%. These observations have different reference periods. Higher market expectations after the outbreak and earlier wage growth cannot together establish that wages had already responded to the war.

The financial section supplied a contemporaneous account of transmission. Between meetings equities had fallen and short-dated euro-area market rates had risen notably. January corporate loan and bond issuance rates had both been 3.6%, with the new mortgage rate at 3.4%. Corporate bank lending slowed to 2.8% annual growth while bond issuance growth increased to 4.0%. Those January figures predated the subsequent shift in financial conditions. The press conference consequently supports a clear distinction between rapid repricing and the much slower arrival of evidence on financing for households and businesses. It also records a separate financial-stability concern. Vice-President de Guindos identified opaque valuation, leverage and redemption gates in private credit, while describing European exposure as smaller than in the United States. He offered no estimate tying that risk to the same-day rate decision.

For a market event study, the conference contained information beyond the hold itself. It revealed that the vote was unanimous, described how energy paths were constructed and explained the fixed policy assumption within the scenarios. The reported equity and rate movements covered the interval since the previous meeting, not a narrow conference window. Any attribution of a yield move to these details requires timestamped prices and an assessment of what markets had already anticipated.

questions.question: How much news came from extending the forecast cut-off?
questions.detail: Compare the two sets of energy and market assumptions as of 4 and 11 March and track which projection components changed. Holding modelling assumptions as constant as possible would show how much of the new central case reflected an extra week of market information rather than a changed estimate of pass-through.

questions.question: Did firms start revising prices more often?
questions.detail: Pair the ECB’s corporate survey evidence on intended price changes with subsequent frequencies of actual resets and sector cost exposure. Separate the fraction of firms repricing from the size of individual changes. Faster revisions across many sectors would provide a more timely signal of propagation than one headline monthly observation.

questions.question: Did the curve reprice the initial energy shock or the likely central-bank response?
questions.detail: Compare near-term inflation compensation with nominal and real forward rates before and after the explanation of the scenarios. Control for commodity-price news during the window. Because the adverse cases hold additional policy fixed, a change in expected policy should be inferred from traded rates, not read directly from scenario inflation.

questions.question: Which differences from 2022 affected wage bargaining first?
questions.detail: Follow contracts negotiated before and after the shock, their indexation provisions and one-off payments. Compare sectors with contrasting employment conditions and energy exposure. Earlier changes in firms’ and workers’ behaviour than the wage tracker projected would change the balance between temporary input inflation and persistent labour costs.
